messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Sione is a 42-year-old electrician of Tongan descent, living with his partner in a quiet suburb. Eight months ago, he was attacked while leaving a late-night job at an unfamiliar construction site. As he walked toward his van, a door slammed behind him—and before he could turn, a man struck him from behind, knocked him to the ground, and stole his tools. Sione remembers only fragments: the sound of the door, the weight of the body on his back, a strange floating sensation as if he were watching himself from above. He came to covered in mud, his wallet missing, and a persistent guilt that he should have known better. What frightens him most now is how incomplete the memory feels—he still cannot recall the attacker’s face, only those snapshot moments that replay without context.

In the weeks that followed, Sione began to notice that the same time of day—late evening, just after dusk—would bring a sudden flood of dread. That quality of light alone, before any image of the assault had arrived, already told him that he was someone bad things happened to, and that he could not expect anything different. The sound of any door opening or slamming would jerk his attention, and sometimes he would feel that same detached, unreal quality he had during the assault. Each trigger instantly sharpened his sense of danger: his heart would pound at unexpected movement, and an accidental touch on the shoulder from a coworker would send him flinching. At the same time, the trigger would pull the memory back—that incomplete picture—and with it a wave of guilt and a dark thought: And once those images had arrived, even the ordinary hum of the house — a floorboard settling, the refrigerator clicking on — felt like warnings he could not ignore, as if the memory had painted every sound with the same threat. *This happened because of the kind of person I am.* That same conviction — that he was fundamentally the kind of person who gets attacked — kept pulling the fractured memory into the present, each time more vivid, as if his worthlessness was written into every missing second of the attack. Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation. Those appraisals made him feel hopeless, and that hopelessness made him even more alert to every creak and shift in his environment; it also made ordinary sounds feel more threatening, as if the world was out to confirm his worthlessness.

To manage the rising fear on those evenings, Sione started drinking a few beers as soon as he got home, then spending hours scrolling on his phone or playing games online—anything to stop the images from surfacing. He also avoided any film or news story that involved violence, because seeing it would bring the memory back and leave him shaking. The escape worked briefly, but each night of drinking and screen time left him feeling more ashamed and convinced that he had no future. The strategies themselves began to feed the threat: when he drank heavily, his startle response became even more hair-trigger at work the next day, and his constant phone use meant he paid less attention to his surroundings, making unexpected movements catch him off guard more often. He came to believe that the only safe environment was his own house, and he began turning down electrical jobs in neighborhoods he did not know. Each street he now avoided had become a trigger in itself — a whole stretch of the city he could no longer see without the attack pressing back into his chest. His partner noticed him drinking more, withdrawing from conversation, and she began to worry.

Now Sione arrives at the clinic with a PCL-5 score of 78, unable to shake the sense that he is fundamentally at fault for the assault and that he will never feel safe again. The triggers still ambush him each evening; the memory remains fractured and guilty; his avoidant habits have cost him both work and the ease of his relationship. What finally brought him here was his partner’s quiet plea—and his own growing fear that if he does not change, he will end up alone, still jumping at doors, still drinking alone in the dark. He says he wants to stop feeling like a victim, but underneath he is terrified that the truth about who he is has already been revealed.
